changes.before: Create a small project with named files and a clear entry point.
changes.after: Keep a program and its instructions together in one clearly named folder.

before: A project is a folder containing files that belong together. A clear entry point tells you which file starts the program. For this project it is main.js. A README is a note explaining what the project does and how to run it. File names and paths matter: a computer does not guess that main.js and main.txt were meant to be the same file.

A code editor lets you change and save files. .js identifies JavaScript source. .md identifies Markdown text, often used for notes. A folder name organizes files but is not itself the program. Save the code before running it: the runtime reads the saved file, so an unsaved editor change may not be what executes.

To try the example locally, create a new folder called greeting-demo and save the example as main.js there. With Node.js installed, run these commands from that folder's parent on macOS:
```bash
cd greeting-demo
ls
node main.js
```
cd changes the current folder; ls lists its files so you can confirm main.js is there; node main.js asks Node to execute that file. You should see the same greeting once. Node is a JavaScript runtime outside the browser. The terminal command is not JavaScript to paste into main.js.

A useful README states the entry point, runtime requirement, launch command, and expected output. Here is example README content, shown as plain text rather than executable code:
```text
Greeting demo
Entry point: main.js
Runtime: Node.js 22.13 or newer
Run from this folder: node main.js
Expected output: Let us build something!
```
Opening README.md lets you read the instructions; executing main.js runs the program. Keeping both files in the same folder makes the project easier to carry to another computer.

For the exercise, set message to exactly Ready to build! and log it once. Capitalization and the exclamation mark are part of the requested output. Repeated console.log calls would produce extra lines. The app's Run action executes your lesson code; it does not automatically create a folder on your computer.

Download main.js and the supplied README.md into your new hello-project folder and open both in your own editor. Check the app's saved-file status before downloading, then verify the downloaded main.js actually contains the current code. If Node is installed, launch it locally and compare the single output line with the README. This completes both the browser exercise and the project-structure practice.
after: A project is a group of files that belong together. Keep them in one folder. The entry point is the file you run first; here it is main.js.
A code editor lets you change files. Save main.js before running it. Node reads the saved file, so unsaved edits will not appear in its output.

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser. With Node installed, open a terminal in the folder containing main.js. Run node main.js. A terminal is a place to type commands; that command belongs there, not inside your JavaScript file.
A README is a note that explains the project. In README.md, name the entry file, required Node version, launch command, and expected output. Keep it beside main.js.
For the browser exercise, set message to exactly Ready to build! and print it once. Keep the capital letters and exclamation mark.

Download your saved main.js and the supplied README.md into a new hello-project folder. Open both files and check their contents. Run node main.js from that folder and compare the one output line with the README.

before.question: You change the greeting in your editor but do not save main.js. Node runs the old greeting. What should you do first?
choices: Edit only README.md to show the new greeting
Save main.js, then run it again
before.explanation: Node reads the saved file, not an unsaved editor buffer. Documentation and folder names do not change the code it executes.

after.question: You edit the greeting but do not save main.js. Node shows the old greeting. What should you do first?
choices: Save main.js, then run it again.
after.explanation: Node runs the saved file. Save your edit so the next run can use it.

changes.before: The app runs your JavaScript file. To finish the project structure step, also create the named folder and open both downloaded files in your own editor.
changes.after: The browser checks the JavaScript output. Creating a folder and running the downloaded files are separate local steps. The supplied README requires Node.js 22.13 or newer.

project.title: A clean starter project
